 North Carolina A&T and UNC Greensboro lack student-accessible early-voting sites
 While both schools have historically had on-campus early-voting locations for presidential elections, they are the only two UNC System schools that do not have sites for the midterm elections. 
 Suhas Nittoor , Escritora 
 • 
 22 de octubre de 2026 
 Grayson Averett 
 Students at several UNC System schools will not have on-campus early-voting locations for the November midterm elections, raising concerns about student voting accessibility.   
 While UNC-Chapel Hill students can vote early at Chapel of the Cross, a two-minute walk from campus on East Franklin Street, the approved Guilford County early-voting plan does not include sites at North Carolina A&T State University or UNC Greensboro.  
 Both schools had early-voting sites during the 2024 presidential election, however, they have not historically had voting sites during midterm elections. 
 Under North Carolina law, county boards of elections develop early-voting plans, which require approval from the N.C. State Board of Elections. If county board members cannot unanimously agree on a plan, they may petition the state board to determine the locations and schedules. 
 Grace Killian, a doctoral student of political science and government at UNC who studies election administration, said universities have limited authority over whether their campuses are selected as voting locations. 
 “Polling precinct location decisions are made at the local level by the local election officials,” she said.  
 Killian said universities can still help students access nearby voting locations through transportation services, including shuttles to polling places that are not within walking distance. 
 The North Carolina Democratic Party is funding a ride to the polls event that will provide transportation every 30 minutes on specific days in October to take voters from NC A&T and UNC Greensboro to the polls for early voting. 
 The exclusion of the two Guilford County campus sites has prompted questions about how election officials balance resources, voter demand and accessibility when selecting early-voting locations. 
 Killian mentioned research shows that moving polling precincts from predominantly Black and brown communities leads to a decrease in voter turnout. Killian added that communities that don’t have access to public transit also see the decline. 
 NC A&T University is a historically Black university and at UNC Greensboro, 54 percent of students identify as people of color in the 2024-25 school year, significantly higher than UNC-CH’s 47 percent of students who identify as people of color in the same year. 
 Frank Baumgartner, the Richard J. Richardson Distinguished Professor of Political Science at UNC, said he believes changes to campus voting locations reflect a broader shift in how elections are administered. 
 “I think now everything about elections is being weaponized in order to manipulate who is more likely or less likely to vote,” Baumgartner said. “Students should understand that there are some people in government who don’t want them to vote in large numbers, and then it becomes incumbent on the people who are being targeted to fight back because it’s a battle.” 
 Killian added that students at NC A&T and UNC Greensboro have challenged the decisions and organized efforts to encourage early voting, potentially offsetting some of the difficulties created by less convenient locations. 
 As for UNC, Chapel of the Cross is one of six early-voting locations in Orange County listed by the Orange County Board of Elections for the 2026 general election. Other nearby locations include Chapel Hill Public Library and Drakeford Library in Carrboro. 
 Micah Mangot, president of the UNC Young Democrats, said the organization has been promoting early voting through outreach in the Pit, including sharing information about voting locations and registration. 
 She said students may not realize that during early voting, they can cast their ballots at any early-voting location in the county where they are registered, while Election Day voters generally must go to their assigned polling places. 
 “We are really trying to insist upon voting early, vote at the Chapel of the Cross, get it done, so that if there are any issues, you can correct it before Election Day,” Mangot said. 
 Matthew Howard, treasurer of the UNC Young Democrats, said changes to absentee voting procedures have also caused confusion among some UNC students. Howard said consistent, clear communication is an important consideration for election officials, particularly when polling locations are moved. 
 North Carolina’s in-person early-voting period began Oct. 15 and ends Oct. 31, ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3. Eligible voters can also register or update their registration during early voting if they provide the required documentation. 
 Baumgartner said the debate over campus polling locations reflects a larger question about the relationship between voters and the officials who represent them. 
 “We want to choose our government,” Baumgartner said. “We don’t want our government to choose who votes and who doesn’t vote.”
